s: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) across three Availability Zones. The database is an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance. The operations team wants to run controlled experiments in production that terminate instances and inject CPU stress, to prove that the recovery actions work. The experiments must stop automatically if the p99 response time that customers see exceeds 800 ms. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
o: Create an AWS Fault Injection Service (AWS FIS) experiment template with an EC2 terminate-instances action and a CPU stress action (an AWS Systems Manager document run by AWS FIS) that target tagged instances. Add a CloudWatch alarm on the ALB p99 TargetResponseTime metric as a stop condition.

Write an AWS Lambda function that terminates random instances on an Amazon EventBridge schedule. Create a second Lambda function that checks ALB latency every minute and disables the EventBridge rule when latency is too high.

Create an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook that terminates instances and runs a CPU stress command. Configure a CloudWatch alarm on p99 latency with an alarm action that cancels the runbook execution.

Use Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) zonal shift to move traffic away from one Availability Zone. Use an Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canary to measure latency and end the zonal shift when latency exceeds 800 ms.

w.y: This is fault injection with a safety brake (exam guide task 3.1: engineering failure scenarios to exercise recovery actions). AWS FIS is the managed service for chaos experiments: an experiment template holds the actions (terminate instances, CPU stress through a Systems Manager document), the targets (selected by tag) and stop conditions. A stop condition is a CloudWatch alarm; when it goes into ALARM, AWS FIS stops the experiment automatically.

o.A: Correct. AWS FIS provides the fault actions, tag-based targets and CloudWatch-alarm stop conditions out of the box, so nothing has to be built or maintained.
o.B: It can work, but it is a home-made chaos tool: two functions to write, secure and maintain, and no built-in stop-and-roll-back safety. More overhead than AWS FIS.
o.C: CloudWatch alarm actions can notify SNS, invoke Lambda, scale, act on EC2 instances or create Systems Manager OpsItems/incidents, but none of them cancels a running Automation execution. The brake would need a custom Lambda function calling StopAutomationExecution, which is extra work instead of a managed stop condition.
o.D: Zonal shift moves traffic away from an Availability Zone; it injects no failure. It does not terminate instances or stress CPU, so recovery is never tested.
